questions.instruction: Compare these two shipping notifications. One is a scam trying to steal your information, and one is a real update.
questions.teaching_point: Identify obvious red flags: generic greetings, suspicious sender domains, and high-pressure urgency combined with non-secure (HTTP) links.

headers.subject: Urgent: Your package is held at our warehouse!

body.content:
Dear Customer,

Your shipment is currently on hold due to a missing house number. If you do not update your information within 24 hours, the package will be returned to the sender.

clues.label: Sender Domain
clues.explanation: The domain 'dhl-ship-info.net' is not the official dhl.com domain.

clues.label: Greeting
clues.explanation: Using 'Dear Customer' is a generic greeting common in phishing.

clues.label: Link
clues.explanation: The link uses 'http' instead of 'https' and points to a suspicious domain.

emails.explanation: This email exhibits classic phishing signs: a generic greeting, a sense of extreme urgency, and a suspicious sender domain and URL.

body.content:
Hello,

Good news! Your shipment with tracking number 840291773 was delivered today at 10:45 AM. You can find the delivery confirmation details below.

clues.label: Sender Domain
clues.explanation: The email comes from the official @dhl.com domain.

clues.label: URL
clues.explanation: The link points directly to the verified dhl.com domain using HTTPS.

emails.explanation: This is a legitimate transactional email. It uses a professional tone, a verified domain, and provides a specific tracking number.

questions.instruction: Review these security alerts. Can you spot the one that is pretending to be Microsoft?
questions.teaching_point: Detect subtle domain variations (look-alike domains) and realize that security alerts rarely ask you to log in via a direct link in the email.

headers.subject: Unusual sign-in activity for your account

body.content: We detected a sign-in attempt from an unrecognized device in Moscow, Russia. If this was not you, please secure your account immediately to prevent unauthorized access.

clues.label: Sender Domain
clues.explanation: The domain 'microsoft-security-alert.com' looks official but is not the actual 'microsoft.com' domain.

clues.label: Link Destination
clues.explanation: The link leads to '.net' instead of the official '.com' Microsoft portal.

emails.explanation: This is a medium-difficulty phish. The branding and tone are professional, but the domain is a look-alike designed to deceive the user.

headers.subject: Security alert for your Microsoft account

body.content: Your password was recently changed. If you did not perform this action, please go to the Microsoft account dashboard to recover your account.
For your security, we recommend visiting account.microsoft.com directly in your browser to manage your security settings.

clues.label: Lack of direct link
clues.explanation: Legitimate security alerts often instruct you to navigate to the official site manually rather than clicking a button.

emails.explanation: This email is legitimate. It uses the official Microsoft domain and avoids forcing the user through a direct link to a login page.

questions.instruction: You receive two emails regarding internal company policy updates from HR. Only one is genuine.
questions.teaching_point: Recognize 'cousin domains' (domains that look similar to the corporate domain) and identify that internal communications should come from the primary corporate domain.

body.content:
Hi everyone,

We have updated the Employee Benefits Handbook for the upcoming 2024 fiscal year. Please review the changes to your health insurance and 401k contributions by the end of the week.

Best regards,
Jane Doe
HR Director, Acme Corp

clues.label: Domain Anomaly
clues.explanation: The sender's domain is @acme-corp-hr.com, whereas the recipient's internal company domain is @acme.com.

clues.label: External Host
clues.explanation: The handbook is hosted on 'share-acmedocs.com' instead of the company's internal SharePoint or intranet.

emails.explanation: This is a highly sophisticated phish. It uses a specific name, correct professional tone, and a plausible 'cousin domain' to trick the employee into thinking it's a specialized HR portal.

body.content:
Hi everyone,

We have updated the Employee Benefits Handbook for the upcoming 2024 fiscal year. Please review the changes to your health insurance and 401k contributions by the end of the week.

Best regards,
Jane Doe
HR Director, Acme Corp

clues.label: Internal Domain
clues.explanation: The sender is using the correct, primary company domain (@acme.com).

clues.label: Official Infrastructure
clues.explanation: The link points to the company's actual SharePoint environment (acme.sharepoint.com).

emails.explanation: This is a legitimate internal email. The sender address matches the company domain, and the link leads to the trusted internal corporate document store.
